answer: The chain turns the integer product into a short-coefficient convolution, moves it onto axes of prime length, replaces each prime-length transform by a power-of-two one (resampling plus Divasov step), runs the power-of-two convolution as a ring convolution whose transforms need only signed shifts, and finally rounds the result back to exact integers. Stage by stage. (1) Radix digits: each n-bit integer is cut into q = ceil(n/b) digits of b = ceil(log2 n) bits. The product then becomes a convolution of length S whose coefficients c_j are short integers below 2^(3b), and S is chosen so that nothing wraps around. This is needed because it makes the final rounding step able to recover exact integers. (2) Address map: S is a product of distinct odd primes. The map Phi rewrites the length-S convolution as one on d axes of pairwise coprime prime lengths s_i, because a transform of length S has no power-of-two structure while coprime axes split into short one-axis transforms. (3) Resampling and Divasov steps: each prime-length transform F_s is re-expressed through a nearby larger power-of-two transform F_t, using an input map A and an output map B_0, so that only power-of-two transforms need a fast algorithm. The permutations are never executed as sorts. The target permutation Q of F_t is absorbed by the Divasov identity Q F_t u = conj(a) times (a convolved with (conj(a) times u)) divided by T, which turns it into one convolution of length T between two phase multiplications. (4) Twist: the convolution over complex arrays is moved onto the ring C[y]/(y^r+1) by the map x_d to zeta*y with zeta = e^(pi i/r). The wrap of the last cyclic axis then becomes a sign, which is repaired by a phase. This is needed because in that ring multiplication by a root of unity (a power of y) is a signed shift of the coefficient list, so transforms over the ring need no complex multiplications. (5) Synthetic-transform convolution: forward synthetic transforms over the ring on the remaining axes, a pointwise record product, and the opposite transform give f*g/T. The forward output is left in bit-reversed order and the opposite transform takes that order as input, so no reordering is run. (6) Assembly: apply Phi to the two digit arrays, apply the resampling-and-Divasov step transform to each, multiply the results pointwise and truncate, apply the opposite transform, scale by S and by 2^(2b+4)S, round to the nearest integers, apply Phi inverse, and propagate radix-2^b carries to get the exact 2n-bit product. The rounding step is licensed by an error bound below 1/2, which I took from the page without opening the page that proves it. Confidence is moderate: the chain of reductions is consistent across the pages I opened, but the resampling identity was imported without proof and I did not check the scale factors beyond the arithmetic shown.

key_idea.statement: Multiplying by Divasov step phases before and after turns a permuted power-of-two-style transform into a single cyclic convolution of length T, so the reordering is absorbed into the convolution and never has to be executed as a sort on tape.

stuck.note: The header lists Babuzif and Muzilef as the convolution routines, but the six numbered steps of the algorithm never name the twist to the polynomial ring. I had to infer from the Babuzif page that the twist sits inside the convolution step, so the place of the twist in the chain was a chain-level gap.

The resampling identity P_s F_s = 2^(2 alpha^2) B_0 P_t F_t A, and the cost and error bounds for A, B_0 and the approximations, are cited to an outside paper and not proved on the page. I accepted them as stated, so their status (proved fact versus assumption) was a statement-level gap for me.
